title: Morkel wants bowlers to embrace Wellington's windy challenge

He has stepped up in the Indian jersey every time he was asked" - Morkel © AFP The Basin Reserve is notorious for its wind, which has long made bowling there as much a test of endurance as skill. Whichever way it blows, one fast bowler has to run in against it, often with little reward. India bowling coach Morne Morkel acknowledged the challenge on the eve of the first Test against New Zealand in Wellington and called upon his bowlers to display “good body language” even when the conditions are tricky in the middle. 
 "That is one of the most talked about topics, I think, even before the start of the tour, the Wellington conditions,” Morkel said. 
 “Again, both teams are going to face the same challenge, so for me, we were quite lucky on Monday that the conditions we faced in terms of getting used to it were quite severe. I feel the boys sort of know what they're in for, but I do believe that it's a matter of just having a strong mindset. 
 “Somebody needs to do the job from one end, and I expect our guys to have good body language in terms of still wanting to bowl and wanting to do a job for the team.”
 The former South Africa fast bowler drew on his own experience of playing at the venue and spoke about how the wind can trouble even the batters. 
 "The way I framed it was that the batter is also standing there, and the wind can blow on his back or knock him off balance,” Morkel said. “So he is going to go through a similar thought process in terms of facing the ball as I am. 
 "For me, I felt like it evened it out a little bit. I do feel at times when you bowl into the wind, there can be a little bit more shape on the ball, it can react a little bit differently. Naturally, with bowling into the wind, you can hold your action a little bit longer, and it can allow you to bowl that slightly fuller length. 
 "Hopefully we won't experience it as severe as it was the last couple of weeks. The forecast is looking quite good. But we've prepared for that, we've spoken about it, and as a bowling unit, we're quite clear in terms of how we're going to take it on."
 With India pushing for a place in the World Test Championship final, Morkel said the series would need a bowler willing to deliver those unglamorous overs.
 "If the moment is crying out for a guy to bowl an extra two or three overs, to play the enforcer role, to do the hard work into the wind, that's going to be needed,” Morkel said. “I just hope we recognise sometimes the guy who's going to do the dirty job into the wind, who's not potentially going to pick up the five-for with the wind. 
 "Ideally, we would like to set the tone in the first session, but you don't need to win the Test match in the first session. Can we string good overs together, and then come day four, day five, somebody puts their hand up and bowls their magical spell? It's going to be one of those series where we need somebody to put their hand up. We've got guys in the change room who can do that on the day."
 Morkel, though, warned against reading too much into the windy conditions. "[Need] not overthink conditions so much,” he said. “I think sometimes we can get caught out with seeing the colour of the wicket, the grass, the wind, looking at stats, and we forget to bowl the ball in the right area consistently enough. 
 "If you look at the stats here, we know guys that can get their lengths right are successful on days one and two, and from there, as soon as the wicket makes a few divots, that comes into play. For us, it's getting as quickly as possible back into the red-ball cricket mindset, back into what our process is that gives us success, and whether we can do that for a long period of time."
 Morkel was also asked whether Mohammed Siraj had slipped down the pecking order, but the bowling coach played the idea down and instead backed the depth of the attack.
 "I wouldn't say that,” Morkel said on Siraj not being an automatic pick in the XI. “I was here with the prep for the Test team, and my feedback to Gautam was that whatever bowling attack we go with on this tour, we've got enough to take 20 wickets. I believe that. I honestly think we've got high quality. So for me, it isn't that one guy is better than another. Each guy brings something different to the bowling attack, and I believe all of them are ready to go. Whatever selection they decide to go with tomorrow, that's up to Shubman and the guys who make the final call. 
 “Coming back to Siraj, for me, he's a world-class performer. He has stepped up in the Indian jersey every time he was asked. But yeah, let's see what we go with tomorrow.”
